title: Nike's $500K Bet on a Rookie Who Wanted Adidas
titleAlternatives: Would you pay triple the record for a rookie?
The rookie who had never worn Nike shoes
Nike lost money, then paid $2.5M for one rookie
Who really signed Michael Jordan? Nobody agrees
description:
In 1984, Nike had just posted its first quarterly loss ever. Reebok was closing in. And Nike was about to offer $500,000 a year, about three times the best shoe deal around, to a rookie who had never played an NBA game and who wanted Adidas.

Today that bet brings in more than five billion dollars a year. But it was less crazy than it looks, and the people involved still disagree about who made the call. Sit in Nike's chair, then find out what happened.

Would you have signed? Tell us in the comments.

thumbnail.headline: Triple the record price
thumbnail.illustration: A faceless silhouette of a young basketball rookie with a name card reading Michael Jordan sits across a desk from a Nike executive silhouette, with a contract and a pen between them and a single pair of plain sneakers on the desk, no logos, 1980s palette.

pinnedComment: You're Nike in 1984: a first-ever quarterly loss, a rookie who wants Adidas, and a price three times the record. Would you have signed? SIGN or PASS, and why?

shorts.hook: Five hundred thousand dollars a year, for a rookie who had never played a single NBA game.
shorts.question: Nike has just posted its first quarterly loss ever, and the kid wants Adidas. Would you sign him?
shorts.reveal: That fall, Michael Jordan signed with Nike: $500,000 a year, his own shoe, and a cut of every pair.

shorts.hook: Nike's goal for the Air Jordan 1 was three million dollars in three years.
shorts.question: Before I tell you what it sold, how much would you guess it made in the first year?
shorts.reveal: More than a hundred million dollars in the first year, over thirty times the goal, in a third of the time.
